definition: Inelastic means not adjusting or responding when conditions such as price change.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inelastic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inelastic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Attendance at the shipyard's licensing exam is inelastic: double the fee and the same three hundred welders sign up, because the license is the only door into the trade.
A sluggish response is slow but real — the quantity drifts eventually, stopping short of inelastic, where the response barely registers at all.
Fixed goes further than inelastic: not a faint response but none whatsoever, the quantity nailed in place whatever the price does.

Unresponsive means failing to react to any push, in any setting — a dead doorbell, a silent help line, a numb audience. Inelastic is the economist's version of that refusal, aimed at one push in particular: price. Demand is inelastic when the price moves hard and the quantity bought barely answers.

Unbudging refuses to shift no matter what leans on it — zero movement, full stop. Inelastic is subtler: an inelastic quantity may twitch when price shoves it, but the response is faint and quickly fades. Unbudging promises perfect stillness; inelastic promises only that the push accomplishes almost nothing.

Engineers spent the morning running elasticity tests on the new cable.
Inelastic means not adjusting or responding when conditions such as price change.
The stadium doubled the price of bottled water in July and sold the same number of bottles; in August it doubled the price again, and the count barely moved.
Thirst in a heat wave, the concessions manager concluded, is almost perfectly inelastic.
Inelastic is more precise than 'steady' or 'unchanging' because it names a relationship, not a state: the quantity people buy refuses to respond when the price moves.
If nothing pushed, 'steady' will do; inelastic means something pushed hard and nothing budged.
Inelastic belongs to economics prose — the SAT loves it near charts about prices.
Keep it for the price-and-demand relationship; for a person who won't bend, use 'inflexible' or 'unbudging' instead.
And note the seam: the in- is a prefix on elastic, making this the one word in the unit where the -ic arrived already attached.

There is one way off Harrow Island that doesn't involve owning a boat: the 6:10 ferry.
So when the operator raised fares forty percent last spring, the islanders' behavior barely moved — ridership that April slipped from 412 daily crossings to 405, then crept back by June.
Demand for the crossing, the county's transit report explained, is almost perfectly inelastic: school, work, and the mainland pharmacy do not become optional because the ticket costs more.
The operator had bet on the same arithmetic, and the higher fares raised revenue almost exactly as projected.
The only real protest was linguistic: islanders now call the boat 'the toll bridge that floats.'
